\chapter{Synthesis --- Reading What You Were Never Taught}
\label{ch:synthesis-friends}
\hlchaptermodality{27}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can read a sentence containing words no lesson has taught me.}

Complete ES-C56-sintesis-leer: read a four-new-word sentence and say what let you read it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Practice]{Synthesis — reading what you were never taught}

\label{lesson:ES-C56-sintesis-leer}



\begin{quote}
You are about to read a sentence with four words in it that this book has never shown you. Read it before you read the explanation.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\begin{quote}
\emph{La \textbf{universidad} tiene una \textbf{reputación} \textbf{internacional}, \textbf{naturalmente}.}
\end{quote}

Say it aloud. Then say what it means.

\emph{The university has an international reputation, naturally.}

Now count what you were given. \textbf{Four of those words are new}, and you read all four:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{universidad} — \emph{-dad} is \emph{-ty}.
  \item \emph{reputación} — \emph{-ción} is \emph{-tion}.
  \item \emph{internacional} — a plain friend; it needed no rule at all.
  \item \emph{naturalmente} — \emph{-mente} is \emph{-ly}.
\end{itemize}

Three chapters of endings, and a sentence of adult Spanish came free.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what has actually changed}]
Something is different about this chapter and it is worth naming.

Every other lesson so far has taught you a word or a form and then asked you to use it. This one asked you to read words \textbf{nobody taught you}, and you could, because a rule reaches further than a word.

That is the shape of the rest of your Spanish, and it is worth expecting. You will keep learning individual words — there is no way around \emph{casa} or \emph{comer} — but the reading you can do will run far ahead of the words you were handed, as long as you keep collecting rules alongside them.

\textbf{A warning that costs nothing.} These endings are reliable, not perfect. A few words wearing a familiar ending have drifted somewhere unexpected, and you will meet them later as \textbf{false friends} — memorable precisely because the rule is otherwise so dependable.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the whole sentence, twice
  \item the four new words alone, and name the rule that gave you each
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many words in that sentence were new? (\textbf{Four}.) What let you read them? (\textbf{Three endings}.) And what does that tell you about the rest of the book? (That \textbf{rules reach further than words} — collect both.)
\end{tcolorbox}
